en: The proof of momentary destruction consists in negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In this context, it is stated that when the reason (*hetu*) exists in the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of negative concomitance implies that which has the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
"Whatever exists is momentary, just like a jar; and these entities under dispute exist"—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

First of all, its lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) is not possible, because the probans—characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), which is intended here by the word "existence"—is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the subject (*dharmin*) as it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), as the case may be.
Nor are there the fallacies of contradiction or inconclusiveness,
because pervasion has been established by a means of valid cognition that sublates the contrary— namely, the non-perception of the pervader—
and the pervader of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is precisely the state of being the object of either successive or simultaneous effects.
Furthermore, neither succession nor non-succession, whether residing in the cause or in the effect, can be its pervaders.
This is because succession, characterized by the act of producing [an effect], is impossible in that which is momentary;
and because the causal capacity is not pervaded by succession and non-succession as they pertain to the effect.

Therefore, the causal power, being pervaded by its objects— effects that are either successive or non-successive according to the nature of the cause— is said to be "pervaded by succession and non-succession.
This is because the locus (the power) is designated by means of its object (the effects),
for the sake of brevity in conventional usage.
And therefore, although it is stated everywhere that succession and simultaneity are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*) of existence (*sattva*), and so forth, nevertheless,
it should be understood that being the object of successive or simultaneous effects alone is the pervader.
Now, when a single effect such as a sprout and the like is produced, [how can this be explained?]
If it is asked, "In that case, how is the distinction between sequential and non-sequential order established regarding the effect?

It is said in reply: although the effect is indeed one and the same, it is designated as "sequential" in relation to effects occurring at different times, and as "non-sequential" due to the absence of such [temporal differentiation]. Thus, its very capacity to produce [effects] constitutes its capacity for sequential and non-sequential production. Nevertheless, because the objects of dependence differ, there is no confusion between the sequential and the non-sequential.
It is like the relationship between father and son.
If it is asked, "What, then, is this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) that establishes pervasion? it is said in reply:
That which lacks the capacity for producing effects either successively or simultaneously is not capable [of causal efficiency],
just like a rabbit's horn.

Furthermore, there is the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha): an entity conceived as eternal cannot possess the property of being the object of effects produced either successively or simultaneously.

This [reason] should not be called "unestablished" (asiddha), because there exists a contradiction between the subject (dharmin) that is eternal and its pervader, which is the state of being the object of successive or simultaneous effects.

For instance, if there were identity between the prior and posterior times, there would be permanence; if there were difference even between two moments, there would be both succession and non-succession.
Consequently, it follows that permanence and the state of being successive or non-successive constitute, respectively, non-difference and difference.
And since these two are characterized by existing through mutual exclusion, they are contradictory.
Therefore, how could succession or simultaneity be possible in that which is eternal?
Nor is [the reason] contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa);
nor is it inconclusive.
Because the absence of succession and simultaneity is pervaded by the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).

For there is no other mode besides succession and simultaneity, by which there might not be a pervasion of causal efficiency by succession and simultaneity when the possibility of causal efficiency exists.

Therefore, because those two [existence and non-existence] are invariably concomitant with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) alone, and because causal efficiency itself is absent when both of them are absent, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the latter by the former two is established. Furthermore,
since the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency is established in the subject (*pakṣa*) through the absence of those two, how can there be any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)?

For there is no other means for establishing the pervasion of the absence of the pervader by the absence of the pervaded, apart from establishing the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader; thus, the non-perception of the pervader is faultless.
It indeed establishes the pervasion of existence by momentariness.

Now, one might object: how can the existence [of a probans] establish its necessary connection with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) on the basis of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), since this [reason] too is corrupted by many defects?

To explain: first of all, this is not a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) reason, because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the subject (*dharmin*) where the property to be proven resides.
Because it lacks establishment through the opponent's own admission,
and because there is no reduction to the opposite [conclusion];
and if, on the other hand, it were independent, [it would be fallacious].
That [reason] is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because a non-momentary locus is either impossible or not cognized.
For cognition must occur either through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).

In the first two positions, if there were causal efficiency characterized by one's own cognition— either directly or through a succession— the primary reason would be "inconclusive" (sādhāraṇa). Furthermore, the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha) would be "unestablished in its own nature" (svarūpāsiddha),
because in the case of causal efficiency, one of the two— succession or simultaneity— necessarily occurs.

In the latter case, however, no reason (*hetu*) would be without a substratum (*anāśraya*), because a subject (*dharmin*) established by mere conceptualization (*vikalpamātra*) is easily available everywhere.
Furthermore, that conceptual cognition must either follow upon perception (*pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvin*) or be produced from a logical mark (*liṅgajanman*).
Whether it be born of mental formations,
or having a doubtful basis,
or being without a basis.
In that regard, in the first two positions, the very existence of the non-momentary is unimpeded; how, then, could a subverting argument (bādhaka) apply?

In the third position, however, there is no total negation of the existence of the non-momentary at all times, because memory of it would be impossible in the absence of the mental impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by it.
In the fourth [case], however, the fault of the reason is that its locus is doubtful.
And in the fifth, the non-existence of its object is not established by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because according to your own view, a non-momentary self is never perceived at all.

Nor can its non-existence be established through inference, because no contradictory mark (liṅga) is perceived; thus, first of all, the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) is raised. In this same manner, the corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) must also be refuted.

This reason is also unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because even for a permanent entity, purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is possible through both successive and simultaneous [operations] depending upon successive and simultaneous auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Nor does the consequence of the faults stated regarding the positions of succession and simultaneity apply;
for instance, it is not contradictory for a thing to produce successive effects depending upon successive auxiliary causes.
And thus, this is Śaṅkara’s concise intention:
for capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed the completeness of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-sākalya*),
while incapacity (*asāmarthya*) is their deficiency (*vaikalya*).
Furthermore, there is no impairment whatsoever to the possessor of those two [manifestation and disappearance] by their appearance or disappearance, because it is distinct from them.
Therefore, how can there be the consequence that it would produce its effect without depending on auxiliary causes?
This is also the condensed meaning of Trilocana:
for it is only the effect that depends upon auxiliary causes,
not the cause of the effect's production.

Since capacity is twofold—both intrinsic and adventitious, which is another auxiliary factor—then even for that which is non-momentary, because there is a multiplicity of successive auxiliaries, a multiplicity of successive effects is also possible; therefore, it is impossible to establish that entities undergo a change of identity at every moment.
Nyāyabhūṣaṇa also says:
"If it is argued that at the time of producing the first effect, [the cause] possesses the nature of producing subsequent effects,
and therefore it should produce all effects at that very first moment."
This is untenable due to self-contradiction, like saying "my mother is barren.
For how could that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect produce that effect at the outset? In that case, it would not have the nature of producing that effect.
For that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth.
Vācaspati also says:
"But surely this non-momentary entity produces its effect by means of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
And since that nature of it exists in the second moment just as it does in the third and subsequent moments, it should produce [the effect] at that time as well."
Or, if it does not act [in the first moment], it would not act even in the third and subsequent moments,
because its state remains the same;
or, if its state is not the same, that itself constitutes its momentariness.
To this it is replied: It is true that [the cause] produces the effect by its own nature, but not by that [nature] alone;
for it is observed that the production of the effect occurs only when [the cause] is accompanied by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).

Therefore, just like pervasion (*vyāpti*), the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must also be understood in one case through the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), and in the other case through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Likewise, because there is agreement among worldly investigators and experts, there is no occasion for the faults mentioned regarding the position that [the cause] produces effects sequentially.
Nor is there room for the faults mentioned regarding the position of simultaneity in the case of non-momentary entities.

For those specific substances that have produced the effect possess an activity capable of producing a restricted effect; once the effect has been produced, even though those substances continue to persist, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) becomes deficient because its purpose has been fulfilled.
How, then, could that which has already been produced produce [anything]?

For the staff and other such instruments are not by their very nature agents, such that they would perform an action starting from the moment of production; rather, they do so by being infused with activity (*vyāpāra*).
Nor is it the case that they are not agents by virtue of their own nature; rather, because they are intent on fulfilling their status as agents through their own nature, they enter into activity.

Furthermore, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), because it would follow that there is an absence of both succession and simultaneity, yet there is no absence of existence.
For it is not established that there exists no other mode besides succession and simultaneity,
since a negation of specific alternatives implies the admission of the remaining possibility.
Furthermore, there is an absolute negation of another mode [of causality] only if it is perceptible;

however, if it is imperceptible, its non-existence cannot be ascertained because of its remoteness. Thus, the pervasion of the capacity for causal efficiency by either succession or simultaneity is not established. Therefore, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) also has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).

Furthermore, because the totality of auxiliary conditions— consisting of both visible and invisible factors— is entirely beyond perception, existence (sattva), which is pervaded by that [succession and simultaneity], is likewise imperceptible; thus,
the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established neither through direct perception nor through inference, owing to the absence of a probans (liṅga) connected to it.
Moreover, it is a most excellent saying that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by both succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*akrama*):
if it is pervaded by succession, how could it be by simultaneity? And if it is by simultaneity, then not by succession.
However, for one who asserts that "it is pervaded by both succession and non-succession," the very absence of pervasion is demonstrated;
for it is not the case that "fire is pervaded by the presence and absence of smoke."
Therefore, the pervasion is inconclusive.
Furthermore, does this subverting argument establish the non-existence of non-momentary things, or rather—
The exclusion of existence from the non-momentary, or else the necessary connection between existence and momentariness—
neither of these two alternatives [is established].
Because, according to the stated sequence, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Nor is the second [alternative] possible;
for the meaning of the term "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) accompanied by the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
And if that [non-existence] were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then it would be its cause; thus, "existence" (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).
The non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). Now, suppose it is conceptualized (*vikalpyate*).
Then, having analyzed it in five ways according to the previously stated sequence, that which is to be analyzed must be refuted;
for this very reason, even the third alternative is not tenable, because when the distinction [of the subject] is unestablished, the relation is unestablished.
Furthermore, here a non-momentary subject (*dharmin*) is not perceived as it is [perceived] in the case of the ground;
nor can the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) be subsumed under the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) without the cognition of some perceptible object.
Moreover, if this [non-perception] were a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*), [it would follow that...]
If it were a property of the substratum, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence;
if it were a property of existence, there would be contradiction; and if it were a property of both, there would be inconclusiveness. Thus, it does not escape these three classes of logical defects.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that there is a contradiction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to the simultaneity of actions in the case of non-momentariness—
one who seeks to establish that contradiction must also understand the contradictory [term].
This is because the establishment of a contradiction is inseparable from the cognition of that [contradictory term].

Just as in the case of cold and fire, or of mutually dependent permanent entities, the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) perceived as non-momentary would have to be real because it performs a cognitive function; for that which does not produce a cognition cannot be an object of knowledge (*aprameya*).
If it is argued that the establishment of contradiction is based on non-momentariness established by conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), [we reply:
even that which is established by convention must be either real or conceptual.
If it is real, how can it be non-existent, and how could there be a contradiction with causal efficiency?
For that which performs causal efficiency is called real.
Or, if it is conceptual?
In that regard, is the contradiction real or conceptual?
It cannot be real, because it is a contradiction of a contradiction that is itself conceptual,
like the contradiction of a barren woman’s son.
Now, if contradiction too is merely conceptual,
then the exclusion of existence is not ultimate, and thus momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is as good as abandoned.
This very series of objections has been summarized by our teachers.

The eternal does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). Furthermore, self-awareness (*svānubhava*) remains unimpaired, and thus the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is also rejected.

Moreover, the void is not established by a second [cognition], nor is non-existence established in the same way as existence. Just as there is no proof of contradiction with the eternal, so too non-existence cannot be established through [the presence of] succession and the like.

To this it is replied: Here, the conventional usage of subject (*dharmin*) and property (*dharma*) is observed even with respect to real entities (*vastu*), such as "cowness in a cow," "whiteness in a cloth," or "motion in a horse," and so forth.

Furthermore, the conventional usage of subject and property is observed even with respect to non-entities (*avastu*), such as "the absence of sharpness in a rabbit's horn," "the absence of crookedness in the son of a barren woman," or "the absence of fragrance in a sky-lotus," and so forth.

In that case, since there is no subjecthood (*dharmitva*) in a non-entity (*avastu*), does this mean that subjecthood is absent by virtue of being a property of an entity (*vastudharma*), or even by virtue of being a property of a non-entity (*avastudharma*)?
In the first alternative, it is a proof of what is already established; in the second alternative, however, there is a contradiction with one's own words.
As the teachers have said:
"Regarding any given object, does there exist here, or not, a mental operation consisting of the affirmation or negation of some property?"
If it exists somewhere, how can there not be so many objections?
If it does not exist at all, then there is the proof of contradiction with one's own words.

The meaning is this: since the absence of the pervader— namely, the prior acceptance of a non-entity as a subject (*dharmin*)— would entail the impossibility of raising the objection of "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*),

it is clearly a feat of divine providence that by the very same statement through which the status of being a property (*dharmatva*) was accepted for a non-entity by means of its lack of being a subject, that very thing is now denied by the opponent.

For instance, regarding the statement "a non-entity lacks the status of being a subject (dharmin)," there are three possible positions: is the absence of the status of being a subject predicated of the non-entity itself, or elsewhere, or is it not predicated of anything at all?

In the first case, there is no negation of the subjecthood (*dharmmitva*) of a non-entity, because the property (*dharma*) consisting in the absence of subjecthood is precisely predicated therein. In the second case, what has happened to the non-entity?

Because the absence of being a subject (*dharmin*) is established elsewhere; however, the third alternative is entirely redundant because it lacks a basis. Thus, how can there be a negation of non-entities being subjects?
Therefore, just as the presentation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is pervaded by the prior acceptance of an object of cognition (*prameya*).
Alternatively, the presentation of a word as a designator (*vācaka*) is pervaded by the prior acceptance of that which is to be designated (*vācya*);
likewise, the presentation of the statement that "a non-entity lacks the status of being a subject (*dharmin*)" is pervaded by the prior acceptance of the non-entity's status as a subject.
Otherwise, the presentation of such a statement would be purposeless.
In that case, if the presentation of the statement is the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*),
then the acceptance of a non-entity as the subject (*dharmin*) is also unavoidably the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*).
On the other hand, if it is not the pervading property, [the objection remains].

In that case, since even the presentation of a statement—which is itself the pervaded—would be impossible, silence would inevitably follow; how then could the contradiction with one's own words not be established? For one who does not speak is not able to inform another, nor is one who speaks able to avoid this fault; thus, one has entered into a great dilemma.
If it is argued that silence alone is appropriate for those with aesthetic sensitivity when the subject under discussion is a non-entity (*avastu*),
oh, what great cleverness!

Having yourself leaped about as much as possible during the discussion of a non-entity, you now wish to escape by the technical term "silence," which is logically the only recourse for one who has been defeated.
Furthermore, a discussion concerning a non-entity cannot be prevented merely by royal punishment or by undesirable consequences such as physical assault;

therefore, even in this case, when the absence of succession and simultaneity is the probans and the absence of existence is the probandum, who can obstruct the status of the subject (*dharmin*)—whether it be a momentary entity whose real nature is doubted or one that is non-existent?
For three kinds of properties (*dharma*) are observed: some are restricted to real entities, such as blue and so forth; [others are restricted to unrealities, and others are common to both].
Some [reasons] are restricted to non-entities, such as the absence of all descriptive attributes;
some are common to both, such as mere non-perception. In that regard, it is logical that the status of being a subject (dharmin) for a non-entity is negated by means of a property of an entity.
It is not [established] by means of a property of a non-entity, nor by means of a property of both entity and non-entity,

because that would entail the consequence of contradicting one's own statement. Therefore, since the status of being the subject (*dharmin*) is unimpeded when there is either absence or doubt regarding the *arkṣāṇaka*, this "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is not an instance of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).
It is rightly said that "we are not perceived as non-momentary" constitutes a reason whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*),
because it is impossible to employ such a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) when there is no perception of it.
However, this perception, which serves as a constituent of linguistic convention, is not of a single form with respect to both real and unreal entities.
For the cognition of a real entity arises either directly or through a succession,
such as perception, inference, and the conceptual construction that follows perception;
however, because a non-entity lacks causal efficacy, its cognition is merely conceptual construction alone.

For regarding a real entity (*vastu*), cognition arises through the power of the entity itself; this occurs either directly as perception (*pratyakṣa*) or indirectly as the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following in its wake, which is inference (*anumāna*).

However, regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), cognition does not arise through the power of an entity, because if it were to act as its cause, it would follow that the thing loses its status as a non-entity.
Therefore, the cognition of a non-entity is merely conceptual construction alone.
For non-existence (abhāva) is not something possessing a physical form that must be directly perceived; rather, it is something to be engaged with through linguistic convention (vyavahāra).
And that conventional usage is indeed established even by conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Otherwise, the conventionally well-known worldly discourse regarding non-entities would not exist.

And since that [non-momentariness] is accepted as being accompanied by the negation of its being an armor (i.e., a real entity), even one who is not an agent must accept that the non-momentary is established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). Therefore, this reason should not be stated as "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) on the grounds of being unperceived.

Consequently, regarding the statement that if the non-momentary is established merely through conceptual construction, no reason would be without a locus because such a subject (*dharmin*) established merely through conceptual construction is easily found everywhere—that is inconsistent; for even if a subject established merely through conceptual construction were possible everywhere, it cannot function as a subject by virtue of being a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*).
Because, with respect to the requirement that a reason must have a real entity as its property (vastudharma), it is possible for a reason to be one whose locus is unestablished (āśrayāsiddha).
For example, the proof adduced to establish the omnipresence (vibhutva) of the self—namely, "because its qualities are perceived everywhere"—is such a case.
Furthermore, this [reason] is a conceptual construction (vikalpa) because of the way the reason was put forward.
Previously, it was characterized by a doubtful subject;
however, once the reason has been established, we say it is "without a subject. Moreover, in this case, what is called "having a doubtful locus" (sandigdhāśrayatva) is not a defect of the reason.
Let this be for now;

for even in the case of a doubtful non-entity, its status as a subject (*dharmin*) is established in relation to properties of a non-entity, since it is established as a subject merely by way of conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
It is precisely with respect to the requirement that a reason be a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*) that a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is defined as one whose locus is doubtful.

Just as here [in the example], "there is a peacock in this bower because of its cry," the non-existence of the object of an unreal conceptualization (avastuka-vikalpa) is established precisely through the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha). In the same way, it should be understood that even for the example— such as space and so forth— the status of being the subject (dharmin) and its cognition occur solely through conceptualization (vikalpamātra).

Thus, since the subjecthood of a real entity with respect to a property that is not a real entity is cognized through mere conceptual construction (vikalpamātra) and cannot be denied, this reason is not one whose locus is unestablished (āśrayāsiddha);
nor is there any deficiency in the example.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*akrama*), which are the two pervaders (*vyāpaka*), are impossible in a non-momentary subject (*dharmin*).

To explain: if it possesses the causal capacity for an effect that occurs in the second and subsequent moments during its first moment, then, like the effect occurring in the first moment, the effect occurring in the second and subsequent moments would also [arise] at that time.
One should [admit that it] acts,
because for that which is capable, delay is impossible.
Alternatively, at that time, the capacity characterized by the completeness of auxiliary causes does not exist.
If it is argued that this is because incapacity, characterized by the deficiency of those [auxiliaries],

is possible— since an entity does not act by its own nature alone, but acts only through its own nature when accompanied by auxiliaries, as we observe the production of an effect only from such a [nature] conjoined with auxiliaries; [we reply:]...

When these [causes], being conjoined, perform an effect, let there be for them this "cooperation" characterized by the performance of a single purpose; who would deny it? But how is it established that the effect must be produced *only* when they are conjoined?
Because the entity possesses the same nature at both earlier and later times.

Because it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that there must always be a fixed rule regarding either production or non-production, the claim of the proponents of permanence—that the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is the producer and not a single factor—is beyond the realm of even their own imagination.
If it is argued, "What can we do? It is simply observed to be so," [we reply:]...

However, let it be observed that this is a point of dispute: whether the production of an effect arises from the very same entity as it existed previously, or rather from something else—a moment produced by a specific collection of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) that has entered into the midst of those conditions.

In this regard, if [the cause] were possible even prior [to the collection], the effect would either be produced at all times or never at all; thus, without resolving this contradiction, one merely asserts the probandum that "the effect arises from that very [cause]. Furthermore, identity is not established through recognition alone.

Because that [personhood] is destroyed again and again—just as hair, *kuśa* grass, or the trunk of a plantain tree is severed—it has been demonstrated by us in detail in the *Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa* (Refutation of the Proof of a Permanent Entity) that recognition is untenable; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
[Objection: But surely it is the effect itself that requires auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*).

But it is not the cause for the production of the effect. If it is argued that capacity is twofold—both innate and adventitious—and that the latter consists of other auxiliary factors (*sahakāri*), therefore, even for a non-momentary entity, there may be a multiplicity of effects occurring sequentially due to the multiplicity of sequential auxiliaries; [we reply: [The opponent continues: If it is argued that... [the rest of the passage follows].

Granted that capacity is twofold, consisting of the innate and the adventitious; nevertheless, that specific individual essence (vastu-svalakṣaṇa) must necessarily be admitted as possessing the property of immediate causal efficiency.
If that [efficiency] were present even previously, then the consequence would be that the effect would also arise previously.
If, on the other hand, it occurs only later, then there is no state of stability at that time.
Nor is it logical to say that an effect depends upon auxiliary causes,
because [the effect] does not yet exist.
Furthermore, if a cause, despite being present, does not produce its own effect, then that very thing cannot be its effect.
Because of its independence.
And as it has been said:
"How could that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect produce an effect at the beginning?"
In that case, it would not have the nature of performing that specific effect;
for indeed, that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth. This [objection] is inconsistent.
If an entity possesses a stable nature, why is it that this effect occurs only at a later time and not at an earlier time?

And since that [earlier effect] is absent, why is it that the cause also has the nature of producing an effect only at a later time? If you say, "What can we do? Its birth occurs only at a later time," [we reply:]...
If it were stable, that [successive production] would be impossible; therefore, let it be designated as unstable.

If it is argued that even in the case of stability, this very nature belongs to it—namely, that it produces an effect only at a subsequent moment—we say no. Because it is improper to accept a nature that is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, for the non-momentary, there is no capacity to produce effects sequentially.
Nor is it possible for [the cause] to produce its effect non-successively;
for if the nature of the causal agent were to persist even in the second moment, there would again be the undesirable consequence of producing an effect.

If it is argued that once the effect has been accomplished, the causal operation directed toward that object no longer exists, and thus the incomplete causal complex cannot produce what has already been produced—this is not so.

Furthermore, since it was already established previously that even in the cases of the presence or absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the capacity to produce is unavoidable whenever the nature of the action and its factors (*kāraka*) is present;
for the very fact that an effect cannot be produced again once it has been accomplished indicates that the cause is incapable.
Therefore, this absence of the capacity to produce effects either successively or simultaneously is not proven in the case of a non-momentary entity.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of another mode [of existence] apart from succession and non-succession, such that—were it not pervaded by those two—the reason would have a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).

For if one were to suspect a third mode, even after refuting both the visible and invisible modes of that [third mode], it would follow that one could not have confidence in one's own position either.
Therefore, since they are established as mutually exclusive, no other mode is possible.
Because a thing, whether real or unreal, that does not enter into the nature of succession is distinct from it;
and because even another mode [of being] does not enter into the nature of succession.

Likewise, although an imperceptible auxiliary cause may be invisible, the pervasion of existence—which is itself perceptible—by both perceptible succession and non-succession is established by perception alone through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), [namely] that existence is necessarily accompanied by a perceptible auxiliary cause.

It is established that causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity; since succession and simultaneity exist through mutual exclusion, the meaning is that causal efficiency does not occur elsewhere apart from these two modes.
Therefore, upon the cessation of these two, [the probandum] would also cease.

As for Trilocana’s three alternatives, the first objection has been refuted by avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). The second is also inconsistent, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is cognized through conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).
For non-existence (*abhāva*) is not something possessing a physical form that must be directly perceived; rather, it is to be dealt with through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone.

Indeed, there is no apprehension of non-existence other than through conceptual construction, nor is there a lack of apprehension; for in either case—whether as apprehension or non-apprehension—it would follow that its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would be lost.
In this way, the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) and the exclusion of the reason (*hetu-vyatireka*) are also understood solely through conceptual construction.
The third objection as well is irrelevant;
for when there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), the pervasion of momentariness by faultlessness remains unimpeded.
Thus, this non-perception of the pervader [establishes] the non-existence of the non-momentary.
It is established that [the reason] proves both the exclusion of the subject from the locus and its pervasion by momentariness, because it consists of a single operation.
Now, if "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) refers merely to non-perception in general, then it cannot produce the cognition of the probandum, because it is a non-entity.

Nor can "perception of something else" be designated as "non-perception of the pervader," since there is no perception of any other thing whatsoever, such as a bare ground. If this is argued, it is inconsistent.

Because the very perception of a property (dharma) elsewhere is established as non-perception [of that property] in another case—for example, in the statement "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees," the perception of the locus (*dharmin*), which is a bare spot, with respect to "trees" is the non-perception of the perceptible; and the perception of the locus, the bare spot, with respect to "the *śiṃśapā*" is itself the perception of the absence of the *śiṃśapā*. Thus, the operation of the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalambha*) culminates in the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

For instance, regarding a permanent subject determined by conceptual cognition, the apprehension of it in its mere state—considering both its successive and non-successive activity—is itself the non-perception of successive and non-successive activity; and with respect to causal efficiency, the mere cognition of it is itself the cognition of its dissociation from causal efficiency. Thus, there is no distinction between this [case] and other types of non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

And with respect to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is the conventional practice of establishing the absence of the pervaded due to the absence of the pervader in an external, non-momentary, unreal object.

Furthermore, conceptual determination should be understood as the capacity to induce activity even toward an ungrasped object, arising from its connection with a specific form acquired through the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Such a conceptual determination has been established in our *Citrādvaitasiddhi*.
And that non-contradictory conventional usage cannot be avoided:
namely, that which is empty of its pervader is not empty of its own nature.
Since this very same point is established by this sequence as well,
and since this logical principle applies just as it does to a real entity (*vastubhūta*), so too to that which is not a real entity— what difference is there?
For it is merely a conceptual construction consisting of a single cognition.
And just as, on the head of a deer, a horn was perceived by him as being associated with it within a single cognition, so too on the head of a hare,
a horn is negated precisely through the possibility of its association with it within a single cognition; likewise,

in the case of blue and other such objects whose status as eternal or non-eternal is not yet established, succession and simultaneity are seen to be associated with their own substratum within a single cognition, even if they were to exist in an eternal entity.

It is on the basis of the possibility that both [existence and non-existence] might be apprehended together by a cognition that grasps [the object] as permanent, along with its own substrate which is likewise permanent,
that the apprehension [of them] through the medium of association with a single cognition is denied.
But how is it that succession and simultaneity do not manifest in a permanent cognition?
If it is argued that we conceptualize the eternal as being precisely that which is encompassed by both succession and simultaneity,
for this very reason there is the application of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), because such an argument would be pointless unless it were to superimpose a contrary nature [upon the object].
Permanence consists in having a single nature throughout different times.
Succession and non-succession exist as distinct forms within two different moments.

Therefore, since eternity and the capacity for successive or non-successive causal efficiency are characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇa*), their contradiction is unavoidable; how, then, could succession and non-succession be included within an eternal entity?

And since they are not included therein, how can there be any mention [of them] when the superimposition (*samāropa*) of succession and non-succession has been removed by the conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) of pure eternity?
Furthermore, even if one were to postulate that the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is eternal,

the non-perception of succession and simultaneity— which are eternally contradictory to it— would simply be its constant perception, since they meet the criterion of being associated within a single cognition;
for this very reason, there is also the non-perception of its causal efficiency (arthakriyā-śakti).
Therefore, because it consists in the perception of a subject that is distinct from the pervader (*vyāpaka*), this [non-perception] is not distinguished from other non-perceptions of the pervader.

If it is argued: "But this is useful as having a non-entity (*avastu*) as its subject, since the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has that as its basis," then what is this so-called "having an entity as its basis"?
Does "having originated from the object" mean (1) even through a succession [of causes],
or (2) being the cause for conventional usage regarding the object in some form, or (3) being dependent upon a real substratum (*dharmin*) that is an actual entity?

If the first position is held, then the fact that [the property of] succession and non-succession, as well as causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), are dependent upon a real entity (*vastu*) that serves as the object for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not undermined. Nor is there any fault possible in the second position either,
because this [argument] is a means for proving the reality of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*).
Nor can even the final alternative be imagined;

for it has been established that the very entity which serves as the subject (*dharmin*) of the conceptualization of permanence is empty of external permanent constituents—whether characterized by succession or non-succession—and is likewise empty of external permanent constituents that possess causal efficacy.

This is because, through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*), there is the possibility of a connection [of the reason] with a subject that is a real entity in the form of a momentary aspect, which is of the nature of cognition.
This very same principle should be applied to such cases as "the speaker is not the son of a barren woman because of the absence of consciousness," and so forth.
By this, Trilocana—who claimed that while [an argument] such as "because of the absence of a tree" can be subsumed [under a specific fallacy], this one cannot—is also refuted.
Furthermore, the absence of sequence and the like does not transcend the three classes of fallacies.

Even if [the property] is a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharma*), the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is avoided. As for what was stated by him— that if the non-existence of eternal things is established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then their being devoid of succession and so forth does not establish the status of being a property of non-existence—
that is a statement difficult even for a child to maintain.
For the subject (dharmin) is eternal;
non-existence is the property to be proven (sādhya);
and the reason (hetu) is the absence of both successive and non-successive causal efficiency.

And its name, "the property of non-existence," refers to its state of being invariably concomitant (avinābhāvitva) with its own probandum, which is characterized by non-existence. And that [invariable concomitance] is established through the pervasion of existence by succession and simultaneity; thus, by the absence of existence—the pervaded—there is the absence of succession and simultaneity.

The absence of the pervader is established as being pervaded; thus, the property of non-existence is established prior to the means of knowledge—whether perception or inference—that establishes the positive pervasion between the two [the probans and the probandum]. Therefore, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Nor does the same consequence apply to non-existence as it does to existence, because the underlying logic is different.
For in that case, both the probandum and the probans are real entities;
therefore, it is logical that their substratum (dharmin) must also be a real entity.
The establishment of a real entity (*vastu*), however, occurs only through perception and inference;
in their absence, there is necessarily a "lack of a locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*), which is logical.

But in the case of proving non-existence, a reason characterized by the properties of a non-entity cannot be refuted by the fault of "lack of a locus," because the subject (*dharmin*)—being a non-entity—is established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
Thus, the contradiction of a non-momentary entity with causal efficiency—whether by way of succession or simultaneity—is indeed established.
Likewise, the non-momentary is established as contradictory solely through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, it must be understood that its nature is nothing other than that which is delineated by such conceptual construction.

Otherwise, it would be improper to negate its being devoid of succession, non-succession, and so forth by referring back to it [as a subject], because its own nature would not have been indicated; this would entail the consequence that words such as "non-momentary" or "rabbit's horn" could not even be uttered. Yet, they do exist.

Therefore, just as the negation of beauty and so forth in the case of the son of a barren woman and the like— which, though lacking any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), exists as a conceptual construction— is appropriate, so too,
what kind of fault could there be in establishing a contradiction between the non-momentary nature itself as presented by conceptual construction and its opposite form?
And if the negation of contradiction [is claimed] because of the absence of experience of the non-momentary, [then...]
In that case, let there be no negation of beauty and so forth simply because the son of a barren woman and such things are not experienced.
If it is argued: "But in this way, contradiction would be non-ultimate;
and by means of that, the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) would also be non-ultimate."

For we do not accept, nor is it logically tenable, that so-called "contradiction" (virodha) is some distinct entity that places its foot upon both sides and is designated as being related [to them]; for if that were the case, then in the absence of reality in one of the two related entities, contradiction itself would be unreal.
However, according to how it is actually accepted, it is indeed ultimately real (pāramārthika).
The meaning of contradiction between two things considered to be opposed is simply their mutual exclusion of each other's essential nature.

And this [exclusion] exists ultimately only in the case of existence and non-existence; it is not that existence enters into the form of non-existence, nor does non-existence enter into the form of existence. This very rule of their non-confusion is what constitutes ultimate contradiction.
For permanence (*nityatva*) consists in having a single uniform nature across different times.

Since succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*akrama*) involve distinct natures even in two moments, there is indeed a contradiction between permanence and the capacity to produce successive or simultaneous effects, just as there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence.
[Objection: But surely, apart from the contradiction between permanence and the possession of succession or simultaneity, there is no other such thing as "contradiction."
If it is asked, "To what does reality belong?", we say: No.
For we do not assert that contradiction is ultimately real by virtue of the existence of some other property (*dharmāntara*).

Rather, when two contradictory properties exist, even if another property named "contradiction" were to exist otherwise, if those two properties are not themselves contradictory, where could there be the existence of ultimate contradiction?
Since the two properties themselves are contradictory, the conventional usage of "contradiction" is established by that alone;
what is the use of another distinct entity called "contradiction," which is established merely by way of a formal proposition?
This, then, is the summary of the prima facie argument.

The eternal does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), one's own experience is undermined, and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is likewise discarded.
Furthermore, emptiness is not established by either [of these two], nor is existence established in the same way as existence itself.
Since contradiction with non-eternality is established, non-existence can also be attributed to succession and the like.

Here is the summary of the established conclusion: Is there, or is there not, in this case, a distinction between negation and affirmation regarding the mental establishment of some property in a given object?
If it exists in some way, how can there not be so many refutations?
If it does not exist at all, then there is the establishment of a contradiction with one's own words.
Thus, that which is permanent is not ultimately real, because it is incompatible with either performing successive effects or performing non-successive effects.

Consequently, even that which is endowed with existence (*sattā*) is not ultimately real. Furthermore, since there is no third category apart from the momentary and the non-momentary, this "existence" (the subject), by being excluded from the non-momentary, comes to rest in momentariness alone; thus, its pervasion is established by the reason of "existence."
The proof of momentary destruction is not contradictory.

That very momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga), which is established through the awakening to the nature of all phenomena as the means for liberation, is the crusher of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthya).
Because the reason is sublated in the case of the opposite [of the probandum], its identity with the probandum is established;
once that is established, the twofold establishment of pervasion (vyāpti) is here described.
Thus concludes the establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) through the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*). // 0 //
